# Building an External Brain for ADHD Productivity

![PLAUD NOTE](permanent/910634513366763929aaf106c37951a9/mem_clFQ5VzCBt/summary_poster/card_20260608054305-v2@32363f17ad00b7dcbad2d9_20260608054430_cd0aec24.png)

This transcript systematically translates ADHD challenges into externalized systems—memory, activation, sequencing, focus, communication, decision-making, and environment—using voice capture tools, AI workflows, timers, blockers, and structured frameworks. It emphasizes accurate tool configurations, weekly reviews, and prompt-driven processes so ideas are reliably captured, time becomes visible, tasks are broken into micro-steps, attention is shielded, communications are offloaded, decisions are scaffolded, and living spaces are managed through small, scheduled actions.
---
## The Memory System: Capturing Ideas Before They Vanish
ADHD brains excel at generating ideas but struggle to retain them long enough to act. The speaker frames working memory as a “whiteboard” that quickly erases—three items instead of seven—making “write it down” unreliable due to distraction and context loss. The remedy is an external memory built on voice-first capture that keeps pace with fast thinking and presents immediate text feedback.

Tools and practices include Plaud for on-the-go capture, Aqua Voice to transcribe and clean speech (removing fillers and false starts) with real-time text output, and consideration of Omni for continuous daily transcription. The speaker advises capturing messily and organizing later—avoiding over-engineered taxonomies—and adding one sentence of contextual detail to each note to prevent future confusion. Weekly 10-minute reviews prevent “digital hoarding” by sorting, deleting, or organizing captured items. Storage will likely be in Obsidian with an AI layer supporting GTD-like retrieval.

The system is positioned as foundational: if memory fails, subsequent systems (time, tasks) collapse. Self-assessment scoring clarifies severity (1–3 rare, 4–6 sometimes, 7–10 constant), underscoring that trying harder won’t fix neurological working memory deficits—external systems are required. Practical guidance culminates in a rapid setup goal to create a voice capture pipeline and first AI-powered notebook within 15 minutes.

---
## The Activation System: Overcoming Time Blindness and Inertia
Time blindness makes “later” feel uniformly distant; ADHD brains often misjudge durations, perceive time as “now” or “not now,” and lose hours unconsciously. The speaker stresses externalizing time through visual and auditory cues so the environment, not willpower, drives activation. RescueTime provides objective data (apps, sites, hours, weekly reports) without manual effort, exposing hidden time sinks (e.g., 2:15 per day on news, 4.5 hours on Reddit, 3 hours on YouTube, 2 hours on inconsequential emails, totaling 18.5 hours weekly).

Visual timers like Time Timer (red disc shrinking) make time tangible and urgent. Keep the timer visible; a minimized or ignored display negates the effect. For non-visual contexts (shower, kitchen), smart home cascades announce time checkpoints (e.g., 40, 30 minutes, and leave now) with distinct sounds, reducing missed commitments. The speaker describes a three-alarm cascade across Alexa/Google Home or escalating phone alarms as an effective punctuality system.

AI scheduling via Reclaim AI blocks deep work, exercise, lunch, and shifts around changes automatically, minimizing calendar “Tetris” and decision fatigue; Motion is a premium alternative that additionally schedules tasks by deadline/priority. Examples include daily client work blocks, afternoon admin, a 30-minute daily walk for “Moki,” and weekly reviews—all protected and rescheduled as needed. Warnings include setting too many alarms (leading to tuning out), using identical alarm sounds (causing non-differentiation), and failing to look at the timer. The ethos favors incremental wins over perfection.

---
## The Sequencing System: Breaking Down Overwhelming Tasks
The speaker reframes task paralysis as a sequencing problem, not a motivation deficit: ADHD brains struggle to identify concrete first steps from abstract goals (e.g., “clean the apartment” contains dozens of hidden subtasks). AI solves this by generating ordered micro-steps with constraints (≤15 minutes, verb-first, numbered like a recipe) based on context (“I have ADHD, I’m struggling to start”). Examples include birthday party planning broken into tiny, executable steps and portfolio redesign guided to a “minimum viable” version (content-only first, no design tool distraction).

Prompts help in multiple scenarios:
- Prioritization: triage tasks into “Must do today,” “Nice to do this week,” and “Can wait or delegate,” then surface a micro-task so small it’s fail-proof (e.g., “open your credit card app”).
- Brain dump sorter: categorize raw thoughts into actual tasks, worries, ideas, and information to remember; then identify what can wait or be skipped.
Goblin Tools (Magic To Do) automatically decomposes tasks with an adjustable detail slider; Todoist offers simple task/due date management. The speaker’s weekly routine uses Claude to sort Sunday brain dumps.

Common pitfalls include never revisiting lists (the list is a map, not the work), making steps too vague (e.g., “research graduate programs”), and trying all tools at once. Recommendations: check only today’s steps each morning; apply the friend test for step clarity; choose one tool for a few weeks; and, when systems break, use a recovery prompt to restart one piece without shame. A 15-minute install suggests using Goblin Tools immediately and saving a reusable breakdown prompt.

---
## The Focus System: Building Shields Against Distraction
ADHD attention automatically follows “interesting things,” often without noticing the shift. The solution is environmental control—remove tempting routes rather than “try harder.” Freedom blocks websites/apps across devices with scheduled sessions (future-self planning), while Cold Turkey offers an aggressive free alternative that’s hard to bypass. Built-in phone features (Screen Time, Digital Wellbeing) provide simple blocks without extra apps.

External accountability via body doubling is effective: Focusmate pairs users in silent 50-minute video sessions so social presence regulates attention. If humans aren’t available, AI check-ins offer lightweight accountability. Work is structured through intervals (Pomodoro: 25 minutes on, 5 minutes off). Breaks should be physical and screen-free to avoid drift. The Forest app gamifies focus by growing virtual trees that die if users leave the app; coins can plant real trees, providing motivational dopamine.

Warnings include checking the phone during breaks, blocking too much (leading to disabling blockers), skipping breaks (leading to crashes), and assuming you’ll remember to start blockers (schedule them). The recommended setup is a blocker list of top distractions, at least one Focusmate session, and a timed focus sprint using Forest or a standard timer.

---
## The Communication System: Navigating Written and Difficult Conversations
Written communication burdens working memory and executive functions—content, tone, format, prior context—without real-time feedback. RSD (rejection sensitive dysphoria) amplifies stakes and hesitation, and time blindness worsens delays, compounding guilt. The speaker advocates a voice-first workflow: dictate responses at 150–180 words/minute (versus ~40 typing), then use AI to convert to concise, professional emails.

Aqua Voice cleans dictation and works everywhere; Gmail’s “Help me write” assists in drafting; Shortwave sorts email noise to highlight important messages (free tier with $14 premium). Templates support common tasks: converting voice to email, fast thread summaries, meeting follow-ups extracting action items/owners/deadlines, clarification requests, overdue replies that avoid over-apology, graceful declines, group coordination with minimal back-and-forth, service provider follow-ups, and concise accountable apologies.

Meeting workflows rely on transcription over handwritten notes, followed by AI extraction and a follow-up email in minutes; notes are organized consistently (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD Topic Key People). Group messaging is managed by muting chats, batch checking 2–3 times daily, and AI summarization to surface mentions that require action; longer responses are voice-dictated then polished.

For difficult conversations, the system offloads preparation: voice dump anxieties, extract core issue/needs/talking points via AI, role-play with adjustable defensiveness, and post-process facts into an action summary to avoid ruminations or memory distortions. The speaker prefers personal handling for deeply emotional matters but acknowledges AI can structure thoughts when needed. Pre-built prompts cover boundaries, accountability, clarification, explaining ADHD’s neurobiology (hyperfocus vs boring tasks), protecting personal systems from unsolicited reorganization, and RSD reality checks. Pitfalls include overscripting, sounding robotic, and using AI to avoid the conversation entirely.

---
## The Decision System: Overcoming Paralysis and Impulsivity
ADHD decisions often swing between impulsivity (ending uncertainty for short-lived relief) and paralysis (over-analysis that masquerades as diligence). Working memory limits, time blindness, and executive function differences impair scenario planning, making external frameworks essential.

Three scaffolds are highlighted:
- 10-10-10: assess emotional impact in 10 hours, practical differences in 10 months, and alignment with values in 10 years—constraining analyses to three concrete horizons.
- Regret Minimization: imagine being 80 and ask which choice you’d regret not taking; flip fear from “what could go wrong” to “what will I wish I had tried.”
- Second-Order Thinking: map “and then what” through cascading consequences, using AI to extend working memory and identify affected stakeholders and hidden problems.

A personal decision (moving back to a smaller owned condo vs staying in a rental post separation) illustrates the framework: stability matters more for kids than house size; worst-case outcomes are recoverable; grief, not logic, caused resistance; AI made patterns and values alignment visible, clarifying the decision. Guidance cautions against overusing frameworks for trivial choices and misusing AI to get answers rather than support thinking.

---
## The Environmental System: Automating a Functional Living Space
Cleaning triggers executive function failures: task sequencing, staying on-track, time estimation, and recent action memory. The method is to reduce cognitive load via the “bouncer principle”—software tells you the two to three specific tasks for today (e.g., wipe counters, vacuum hallway), deferring everything else.

Hardware like robot vacuums can remove tasks entirely if budget allows; however, software is cheaper and often sufficient. Sweepy breaks the home into 2–5 minute tasks, uses AI to calculate urgency based on time since last clean and typical dirt accumulation, and gamifies the process with points and leaderboards (family participation supported; premium $24.99, free for solo use). Tody (one-time $6.99) presents due tasks visually and features a motivational mascot. AI assistants can serve as free alternatives using the same decomposition prompts. The “good enough” framework argues that perfection is neither necessary nor strategic—functional, manageable spaces reduce shame and cognitive drain.
